note: First batch: picked from PubMed by publication date, 16 Oct to 16 Nov 2026, before the topic split.

items.title: Right putaminal gray matter change tracks psychomotor recovery after accelerated iTBS in melancholic treatment-resistant depression
points: Test whether putamen volume change tracks early psychomotor recovery after accelerated theta-burst stimulation (iTBS) in melancholic treatment-resistant depression.
Structural MRI (voxel-based morphometry) in 61 patients and 77 controls, then a double-blind, sham-controlled trial of 20 sessions over four days; 50 patients had complete data.
Patients had more right putamen volume at baseline. After active stimulation, putamen increase tracked psychomotor improvement, but not overall depression, and the link was absent after sham.
The authors frame the change as a possible marker of early psychomotor recovery, not as structural normalisation.
Correlational; 25 patients per arm; the psychomotor link is a secondary pattern.

items.title: Deep brain stimulation of the nucleus basalis magnocellularis ameliorates autistic behavior in a rat model of autism via cholinergic modulation in the prefrontal cortex
points: Test whether stimulating the nucleus basalis magnocellularis improves autism-like behaviour in a prenatal valproic-acid rat model.

Male offspring were split into control, VPA, implanted-only and stimulated groups; stimulation ran two hours a day for two weeks, with behaviour tests and acetylcholinesterase and choline acetyltransferase staining.
Stimulation improved social behaviour and increased acetylcholinesterase-positive neurons in the medial prefrontal cortex.
The benefit is linked to cholinergic signalling in prefrontal cortex, supporting a basal-forebrain route for DBS effects.
Animal model; small groups (five saline controls, 16 VPA-exposed rats); the marker link is correlational.

items.title: Treatment-characteristic brain structural changes in depression: a multi-center longitudinal observational study
points: Compare how grey matter volume changes across four depression treatments: medication, CBT, ECT and rTMS.
155 patients and 152 controls with MRI at three timepoints; voxel-based morphometry with ComBat scanner harmonisation.
Only ECT and medication changed grey matter over time; CBT and rTMS did not, although all four groups improved clinically. Later left insula loss correlated with worsening on medication.
Treatments leave different structural signatures, and the insula could serve as a long-term biomarker.
Observational design; the rTMS arm had only 20 patients.

items.title: Association of high-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation with 6-month cognitive outcomes and white matter lesion progression in patients with cerebral small vessel disease and cognitive impairment
points: Assess whether 10 Hz rTMS over the left DLPFC relates to six-month cognitive outcomes and white matter lesion progression in small vessel disease.
Retrospective cohort of 427 patients (228 rTMS, 199 medication-only) with complete data; primary outcome was change in MoCA; propensity-matched sensitivity analysis.
The rTMS group gained more on MoCA (mean difference 1.11), with better MMSE, TMT-B and delayed recall; no imaging difference was significant.
Cognitive benefit may come from plasticity and network changes rather than from slowing lesion growth.
Retrospective and based on routine care; subgroup findings are exploratory.

items.title: Deep-brain Neuromodulation in Parkinson's Disease: Convergent Mechanisms and Translational Stratification of Deep Brain Stimulation and Low-intensity Focused Ultrasound
points: Compare DBS and low-intensity focused ultrasound as deep-brain approaches in Parkinson's disease, looking at mechanisms.
Mechanistic and translational review of clinical and preclinical evidence.
The two share some mechanisms, including network modulation, synaptic remodelling and reduced neuroinflammation. DBS has far stronger clinical evidence.
Deep-brain neuromodulation should be viewed as one multi-dimensional framework, with biomarkers and standard endpoints needed.
A narrative review, not systematic; clinical ultrasound evidence is still limited.

items.title: Implantation of autologous peripheral nerve tissue to the nucleus basalis of Meynert in patients with Parkinson's disease during deep brain stimulation surgery: a 2-year report
points: Assess the safety, feasibility and clinical response of placing a nerve graft in the nucleus basalis during DBS surgery.
Seven patients had pallidal DBS plus a sural nerve graft to the nucleus basalis, followed at six-month intervals for up to two years (five completed 24 months).
No serious related adverse events; cognition matched standard DBS patients; motor and quality-of-life scores were slightly worse, with small non-motor gains.
The procedure appears safe and feasible without a substantial added cognitive risk, and the authors suggest possible target-specific effects.
Seven patients, no control group, and fewer patients at 24 months.

items.title: Outcomes of Bilateral Globus Pallidus Internus Deep Brain Stimulation in GNAO1-Related Disorder: An International Multicenter Experience
points: Define the impact of bilateral pallidal DBS in GNAO1-related movement disorder, the largest cohort to date.
Retrospective multicentre cohort of 46 patients across 17 centres, with a mean follow-up of 4.5 years; primary outcome was dyskinetic crisis burden.
Crises fell in 38 of 40 patients, and motor scores improved by about 27.5%; complications occurred in 19.6%, mostly in emergency implants.
DBS works mainly to prevent crises and reduce overall burden, rather than restoring function, which supports earlier elective surgery.
Retrospective; functional classification was largely unchanged.

items.title: Deep brain stimulation of the nucleus accumbens for severe self-injurious behaviour in children: long-term outcomes from a first-in-human pilot trial
points: Report long-term outcomes of accumbens DBS for severe self-injury in children with autism.
Single-centre first-in-human trial: six participants aged 7–14, bilateral implantation, followed for at least 24 months (mean 32.5).
Self-injury frequency and severity fell and stayed low; one device infection led to relapse, which reversed after re-implantation.
Modulating reward circuitry may durably change maladaptive behaviour in childhood neurodevelopmental disorders.
Six patients; single centre; the withdrawal-rechallenge evidence rests on one participant.

items.title: Changes in the Cutaneous Silent Period Following Pallidal Deep Brain Stimulation in Patients with Cervical Dystonia
points: Track spinal inhibition, measured by the cutaneous silent period, before and after pallidal DBS in cervical dystonia.
18 patients measured before and after bilateral GPi-DBS, compared with 18 matched healthy controls.
Silent-period end latency and duration increased early after surgery while stimulation was on; neither timepoint differed from controls, and changes did not track clinical improvement.
Spinal inhibition appears to shift dynamically during active DBS, linked to wider motor-network modulation.
Small sample; short-term follow-up; no correlation with clinical gains.

items.title: Effects of STN-DBS on voluntary facial mimicry in Parkinson's patients: a pilot study
points: Test whether subthalamic DBS changes voluntary facial expressiveness in Parkinson's disease.
18 patients recorded in stimulation-on and stimulation-off states (both on medication) while posing six basic emotions and neutral; facial action units were scored automatically.
Motor scores improved with stimulation. Mimicry was weaker with stimulation off for neutral, happiness, fear and anger, and stronger for sadness.
Subthalamic DBS seems to shape emotional motor output beyond classic motor control, which may help social communication.
Pilot size; a single within-patient comparison.

items.title: Applications of non-invasive brain stimulation in the treatment of children with cerebral palsy: a narrative review
points: Summarise evidence for tDCS and rTMS in children with cerebral palsy.
Narrative review informed by a structured literature search.

Small to moderate trials suggest added benefit for gross motor function, gait, balance, spasticity and some cognitive and communication outcomes when paired with rehabilitation; short-term safety was acceptable.
Targets include primary motor, dorsolateral prefrontal and language cortex, with plasticity-based mechanisms and individualised protocols.
Not systematic; safety data are short-term.

items.title: The Pallidothalamic Tract in Functional Neurosurgery: A Systematic Review
points: Synthesise outcomes of interventions targeting the pallidothalamic tract.
PRISMA 2020, PROSPERO-registered; 40 studies and 483 patients across five modalities, including MR-guided focused ultrasound, DBS, radiofrequency and lesioning.
Average UPDRS-III improvement of 39% in Parkinson's disease, 57% on BFMDRS in dystonia, and seizure reduction in 71% of drug-resistant epilepsy patients.
Dual-target strategies may add benefit, and prospective trials are needed to confirm efficacy and safety.
Mostly small uncontrolled studies; inconsistent adverse-event reporting.

items.title: Dopamine amplifies subthalamic long-latency responses to cortical stimulation in patients with Parkinson's disease
points: Determine how dopamine affects signal flow along the cortico-subthalamic hyperdirect pathway.
Bidirectional stimulation with invasive recordings in 15 patients undergoing DBS surgery, across medication states.
The short-latency hyperdirect response was unchanged by medication; later responses were amplified by dopamine; subthalamic-to-cortex responses were unchanged.
Fast and slow components of cortex-basal ganglia communication are affected differently by dopamine.

items.title: Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation (tDCS) and Smoking Cessation: Clinical and Neurocognitive Outcomes Among Turkish Adults
points: Test whether anodal tDCS over the left DLPFC helps smokers quit, and whether it changes executive function.
Active versus sham tDCS in smokers with high nicotine dependence, one session per day, five days a week for two weeks; executive tests before and after; weekly follow-up for a month.
No significant group difference in smoking outcomes or clinical measures after adjusting for baseline imbalance, and no difference on executive tests.
tDCS was not effective for smoking cessation here, and the null executive result runs against the wider DLPFC literature.
Modest sample; baseline groups differed on smoking measures; context may differ from other populations.
